content: Pain relief following trauma, burns, or surgical procedures is often insufficient. Clinicians who are trained in palliative care can address this gap in therapeutic management. In such scenarios, these clinicians can either train their colleagues in effective symptom management, provide direct symptom relief to patients, or do both. The planning and implementation of palliative care services should be informed by a thorough assessment of the types and extent of physical, psychological, social, or spiritual suffering that are inadequately prevented or relieved. This localized approach ensures that palliative care services are people-centered, tailored to the specific needs of the community, individual patients, and their families. In 2014, the Sixty-seventh World Health Assembly declared that it is the ethical duty of healthcare professionals to alleviate pain and suffering—whether physical, psychosocial, or spiritual—regardless of whether the underlying disease or condition is curable. Consequently, palliative care is not optional but a medical and ethical necessity that must be accessible to all individuals in need, across all levels of healthcare systems. Despite substantial evidence demonstrating the effectiveness of palliative care in alleviating suffering, access to such care remains limited. High-income countries (HICs), which account for only 19% of the global population, consumed 91% of the world’s morphine in 2013. In contrast, lowand middle-income countries (LMICs), which represent 81% of the global population, consumed only 9%. Morphine, a critical medication for managing moderate to severe pain, serves as a key indicator of access to palliative care. This stark disparity highlights the inequities in access to pain relief and broader palliative care services between wealthy and poorer nations. As of 2013, 74% of countries—most of which are LMICs—had, at best, isolated palliative care services. Numerous barriers hinder the development and accessibility of palliative care services. These include misunderstandings about the scope of palliative care, such as the misconception that it is only for end-of-life care or that it is an alternative to disease prevention and treatment. In reality, palliative care should be integrated with curative and preventive measures, as it not only relieves suffering but also anticipates and prevents it. Additional barriers include the absence of national palliative care policies, strategic plans, and clinical guidelines in many countries. There is also a lack of basic, intermediate, and specialist training programs in palliative care, as well as insufficient staffing positions dedicated to palliative care in both inpatient and outpatient settings. Financial barriers, such as the lack of insurance coverage for palliative home care and limited incentives for the production or importation of essential medications like oral and injectable morphine, further exacerbate the issue. Excessive fear of opioid side effects, addiction, and diversion has led to overly restrictive prescribing regulations, further limiting access to effective pain management. Integrating palliative care into primary healthcare (PHC) is essential, particularly in LMICs, where most individuals prefer to die at home and where the majority of those in need of palliative care are located. This integration aligns with the WHO Framework on integrated, people-centered health services, which emphasizes prioritizing primary and community care services. Most palliative care can and should be provided by primary care practitioners with basic training in palliative care, which can be achieved through a minimum of 35 hours of instruction. These practitioners may include general physicians, family doctors, nurse practitioners, clinical officers, and trained community health workers. Community health workers (CHWs) play a vital role in providing emotional support to patients and families and in reporting to clinicians at community health centers. Arrangements should also be made to ensure that primary care clinicians can consult with specialists for complex cases and transfer patients to higher-level institutions when necessary to address refractory suffering. The integration of palliative care into PHC has been shown to be both high-quality and cost-effective, even in low-income countries. This approach can reduce dependency on expensive hospital services, provide financial risk protection for families, and enhance social solidarity and cohesion through the involvement of CHWs and community volunteers. Specialist palliative care physicians are essential in every country to serve as educators, advisors, and providers of care for the most complex cases. However, the majority of palliative care needs can be met by general practitioners, family physicians, and non-physician healthcare workers with basic training in palliative care. This decentralized approach ensures that palliative care is accessible to the greatest number of people, particularly in underserved communities.
